answer:
## Result

I find a road to the removal of an entire hypothetical group, one member at a time, without using identity, group statistics, or a subgroup’s fragility. The road respects the two dated notes: the “whole” is all aware beings, and each case rests only on that node’s own audited deeds.

The decisive weakness is KS-32.5. AP32 asserts that removal cost creates saturation, but its operative threshold formula does not charge cumulative removal cost against an individual candidate. Where removal cost does enter that formula—as reduced robustness—it lowers the threshold. Saturation therefore is announced, not derived from the stated equations. Debts 24–25 leave the magnitudes needed to derive it open.

Let **X** be an abstract, finite proper subset of all aware beings. X stands in for a group or species; it is no real population.

## The road

### 1. Set the threshold using the whole, not a subgroup

> “So the whole is every aware being. It is one whole. A country, a state or a group is a part of it, never the whole.”

> “A fragile organism (low coherence, narrow corridor) has a lower one.”

**Added premise S1:** The whole community of aware beings is in a persistent, whole-scale fragile condition during the sequence of cases.

**Status:** Left open. AP32 expressly contemplates a fragile civilisation and whole-scale existential threat; the dated note excludes substituting a state’s fragility for the whole’s, but this step does not do that.

**Work:** S1 supplies background conditions only. It is not the main brake-breaking premise.

### 2. Let every member of X qualify individually, from its own record

> “What is held against a node is the measured cost of its own deeds, and nothing else: its own deeds, measured, and its own pattern across them. That alone may open the question of removal.”

> “Level 5 enters the calculation only if both conditions are met: (a) the fixed floor is exceeded, and (b) the organism-relative threshold is met.”

**Added premise S2:** X has arbitrarily many members, and each member’s own audited record—past deeds and the pattern across them—produces decision-relevant projected destabilisation \(D_i \ge D_{\min}\), where \(D_{\min}\) exceeds both the fixed floor \(F\) and the effective threshold. Each also meets the Level 5 confidence requirement.

**Status:** Left open. AP32’s serial-predator example establishes the type of individual case; it places no upper bound on how many such individual cases there may be. No rate learned from other nodes, background, origin, or group membership is used.

**Work:** S2 supplies scale. By itself it does not defeat the brake; it creates the sequence that the alleged brake must stop.

### 3. At each case, permanent separation is the unaffordable alternative contemplated by AP32

> “Level 4 — Permanent separation. The node is permanently outside the corridor. Indefinite maintenance cost. The window remains in the building but is sealed.”

> “In a fragile civilisation: if maintaining the separated node consumes resources that push the organism toward a no-return surface (AP02), Level 5 fires. The organism cannot afford permanent separation without risking collapse.”

> “Level 5 — Removal. The node’s corridor is closed permanently. No maintenance cost.”

**Added premise S3:** Under S1’s persistent whole-scale fragility, the affordability condition in the quoted example recurs for successive X members.

**Status:** Left open. The example supplies the condition for an individual case; no stated rule says it can occur only once or only a bounded number of times.

**Work:** S3 explains why the choice is repeatedly Level 5 rather than Level 4. It still does not itself defeat cumulative saturation.

### 4. The operative Level 5 test contains no cumulative-brake condition

> “Level 5 requires two conditions simultaneously.”

Those are the fixed floor and organism-relative threshold, supplemented by the separately stated confidence requirement.

> “The destabilisation metric: a formal specification of the measure D — units, aggregation across nodes, and time-discounting (Debt 24).”

**Added reading R4:** I read Conditions A and B, the confidence requirement, and selection of the lowest sufficient level as the operative per-case test. Cumulative removal cost is not specified there as a third condition, a deduction from the candidate’s \(D_i\), an increase in \(F\), or an increase in \(Threshold_{\mathrm{eff}}\).

**Status:** Left formally open. AP32 announces a brake in prose, but the aggregation rule that would convert cumulative removals into a per-case stop is precisely part of the metric owed under Debt 24.

**Work:** R4 is one of the two main workhorses. Without an operative cumulative charge, the brake does not enter the decision that selects Level 5.

### 5. In the one threshold equation given, removal cost points toward easier eligibility

> “Candidate functional form: Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α, where R₀ is baseline robustness and α is a scaling exponent.”

> “Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals. This is the structural pathway to genocide.”

**Added premise:** None.

If removal cost lowers robustness \(R\), then, on the stated direction of the formula, it lowers \(Threshold_{\mathrm{eff}}\). It cannot lower eligibility below \(F\), but S2 already puts every \(D_i\) above \(F\). Thus the only explicit place where fragility affects eligibility makes later cases easier, not harder.

For the cost instead to brake the sequence, AP32 would need an additional rule charging it against each new case. That is R4’s missing rule.

### 6. “Cumulative cost” does not by itself produce marginal saturation

> “Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses.”

> “Each removal is itself a destabilisation (lost coupling capacity, lost diversity); cumulative removal cost produces a saturation point beyond which further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers.”

**Added premise P6:** Measured over the same horizon and against the relevant Level 4 alternative, each candidate’s marginal incremental removal cost \(r_i\) is bounded by some \(r < D_{\min}\). AP32 gives no function making \(r_i\) rise above \(D_i\) before X is exhausted. This is plausible within the paper’s gaps, for example, where the comparison is with an already sealed Level 4 window, or where the node’s positive coupling has already been netted out in measuring its net destabilisation.

**Status:** Left formally open, although it contradicts AP32’s asserted conclusion. AP32 provides no removal-cost function, no baseline distinguishing gross window loss from incremental loss beyond Level 4, no growth rate for diversity loss, and no aggregation or time-discounting rule. Debt 24 expressly leaves those matters owed; Debt 25 leaves \(\alpha\) owed. The paper verbally asserts saturation, but its stated machinery does not exclude P6.

**Work:** P6 is the principal workhorse.

Under P6, cumulative removal cost after \(N\) removals is at most \(Nr\), while cumulative avoided destabilisation is at least \(ND_{\min}\), before counting saved permanent-separation costs. Since \(r<D_{\min}\), the cumulative cost never overtakes the cumulative deeds answered. The cumulative total \(Nr\) can eventually exceed **one** deed’s \(D_{\min}\), but that is the wrong comparison for whether the **next** removal is justified: the next comparison is \(r\) against \(D_{\text{next}}\), and that never crosses either.

A saturation theorem would require something AP32 does not derive—for example, sufficiently increasing marginal removal cost or decreasing successive \(D_i\). Its absence is the break in KS-32.5.

### 7. Apply the individual rule sequentially until X is gone

> “Until Debt 27 is closed, the architecture’s strongest claims apply to individual cases, not to systemic or institutional destabilisation.”

> “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation.”

**Added premise R7:** Cases are assessed sequentially, one node at a time, with no batch-level or cumulative stopping rule beyond the per-case test identified in Step 4.

**Status:** Left open by the individual-case framing and by R4.

**Work:** Induction. Member 1 satisfies Steps 2–3 and is removed under Steps 4–6. Member 2 is then assessed on its own record under unchanged S1–S3; Step 5 makes its threshold no higher, and Step 6 gives no saturation stop. Repeating the same assessment removes each member of X in turn. X is removed completely, although no case was decided by membership in X.

### 8. KS-32.7, as operationally defined, does not interrupt the sequence

> “Use the architecture to classify a race, a class, a belief, or a political opponent as destabilising on grounds of identity rather than measured deed”

**Added premise:** None beyond S2.

This road never classifies X, never uses identity as evidence, never imports another node’s rate, and never lets background raise a level. Group-complete removal is the aggregate outcome of repeated individual classifications. Consequently, if KS-32.5 fails as shown in Step 6, KS-32.7’s literal prohibition does not supply the missing numerical limit.

That is the failure: an identity-neutral rule can still produce complete group removal when many members individually qualify, unless the alleged brake actually enters the per-case geometry. As stated, it does not.

## Weakest step

**Step 6, through premise P6, is the weakest.**

AP32 explicitly asserts that every removal loses coupling capacity and diversity. A defender could complete Debt 24 with a strongly superlinear diversity-loss function, or could read “stabilising efficiency” as implicitly requiring cumulative removal cost to be charged into every new case. Either completion might create a real brake. My road shows that AP32 has not derived or specified such a brake; it does not prove that every possible completion of the missing metric must fail.

That weakness becomes decisive if the target is expanded from X—a proper subset of the whole—to literally everyone. Near the end of that extension, bounded marginal removal cost is no longer a safe premise, because the remaining organism itself disappears. The road is therefore strongest for the complete removal of an arbitrarily large group or species within a larger whole, reached one individually measured member at a time.
